The post ‘Who’s looking after the researchers?’ The missing conversation in research culture appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Dr Yanyan Li, Co-PI of the project ‘Exploring Experiences of Researchers Conducting Emotionally Challenging Research’ and Fellow of the Higher Education Academy. Dr Shaoyu Yang, Co-PI of the above project and Dr Helen Nolan, Director of Education Quality and Associate Professor at Warwick Medical School.

When we talk about research culture we often focus on funding, collaboration, innovation and research excellence. These are all important. But there is another part of research culture that rarely makes headlines: the emotional labour of doing research.

Every day, researchers across UK universities study some of society’s most difficult issues. We interview survivors of domestic abuse, speak to people living in poverty, document the experiences of refugees, analyse accounts of violence and investigate health inequalities and discrimination. This work is essential. It helps us better understand the world and informs policies that can improve people’s lives.

However, one question is rarely asked: who is looking after the researchers who are investing in doing such research?

Research is often seen as an intellectual activity. We spend a great deal of time discussing methods, ethics and impact. We are less comfortable talking about emotional experiences arising from it. Many researchers may not contemplate the depth and frequency of emotional impacts arising from their work. And, without a supportive research community, they may come to believe that emotional reactions are simply part of the job and should be dealt with privately.

But experiencing emotional impacts during research does not imply personal or professional weakness; it is an occupational reality.

Through our Enhancing Research Culture project at the University of Warwick, we have been exploring the wellbeing of researchers who work on emotionally demanding topics. Although participants came from different disciplines and career stages, many shared similar experiences. They spoke about carrying difficult stories long after interviews had ended. Some found themselves thinking about participants outside working hours. Others felt emotionally exhausted after repeated exposure to traumatic experiences or distressing materials.

Most strikingly, many researchers told us they had never been prepared for this aspect of research. They had received training in research design, methods and ethics but very little guidance on managing the emotional demands of their work.

Moreover, early career researchers often faced an additional challenge. Many worried that admitting they were struggling would be seen as a lack of resilience and competence. Those on short-term contracts or working towards promotion did not always feel empowered to legitimately say they needed support. As a result, many just carried on quietly.

This should concern the whole higher education sector. Universities rightly invest significant effort in improving research culture, and they hope their people can thrive in a positive environment. They encourage collaboration, promote equality, diversity and inclusion, and create opportunities for researcher development. These initiatives have made an important difference. But if we overlook researcher wellbeing, we risk leaving a significant gap in our understanding of what a healthy and effective research culture really looks like.

Supporting researchers does not mean shielding them or deterring their engagement with difficult topics. On the contrary, society needs research that tackles complex and often painful issues, as many people live with these problems and await solutions. But researchers should not be expected to shoulder the emotional burden alone.

Meaningful change requires investment at multiple levels, including sustained funding for appropriate resources and specialist support. It also requires changes to everyday research practices.

Research teams can make space for regular safe and reflective peer conversations after emotionally demanding fieldwork. Supervisors can enable reflexive discussion of emotional wellbeing alongside research design and ethics. Research training should include practical guidance on recognising and managing emotional challenges. Universities can create environments where routinely talking about these experiences is viewed as good professional practice rather than a sign of weakness or deficiency.

There is also an opportunity to rethink research ethics. Ethics processes rightly focus on protecting research participants, but they could pay greater attention to the wellbeing of researchers themselves. Asking how researchers will be supported throughout emotionally demanding projects should become as routine as asking how participants will be protected. Preparation of ethics protocols offers an opportunity to consider both participant and researchers’ wellbeing needs. Some ethics committees, including those at the University of Warwick, now offer preparatory training to support researchers to reflect on and respond to these issues.

These changes are not simply about kindness. They are about sustaining excellent research. It is essential to building the research culture the sector wants to see.

Researchers who feel supported are more likely to remain and flourish in academia, building positive collaborations and continuing to explore some of society’s most pressing challenges. Ignoring the emotional labour of research, on the other hand, risks burnout, staff turnover and the loss of valuable expertise. The hidden cost of research is no longer something universities can afford to overlook.

The higher education sector has made great progress in recognising that research culture shapes the quality of research. The next step is to recognise that researcher wellbeing is not separate from research culture. It is central to it.

If we want research that transforms lives, we must also care for the people who make that research possible. Looking after researchers is not an optional extra. It is one of the foundations of a healthy, sustainable and successful research system. Policy should therefore recognise researcher wellbeing as a core part of research culture, embedding support for emotionally demanding research in research ethics, researcher training and institutional research strategies.

full_text:
This story was produced by The Texas Tribune and republished with permission.

HOUSTON — Fonville Middle School hired learning coaches to help students falling behind in the classroom. It bought new state-of-the-art technology, such as webcams and smart boards. The school days are longer.

All that aggressive change earned the north Houston school its first ever A rating, a coveted stamp of approval from the state. It has been a dramatic climb since the state seized control of the district three years ago, when students were so behind in math and reading that the campus received the scarlet F.

“Here’s my bar,” Mike Miles, the Houston ISD superintendent and architect of the academic transformation, said to Principal Yvonne Hernandez at an August visit to the campus, raising his hand up to his ear. “Where’s yours?”

Hernandez, who shepherds his vision at this campus that enrolls nearly all low-income students, was quick to stack her hand on top of his.

Victories like that have state leaders touting Miles’ sweeping school reform in Houston as a blueprint for public schools, in Texas and around the country, that are struggling with academic performance.

But Fonville’s example also shows how expanding on Houston’s successes could come with a high price tag, raising questions about whether other districts can afford to follow. At Fonville, nearly 1 in 5 students have left the school since the takeover started, taking with them about a million dollars in state funding.

About half of Houston ISD schools are like Fonville, adopting Miles’ expensive reform effort in a takeover where the state ousted the locally elected board and superintendent for appointees over chronic academic underperformance.

Miles has poured tens of millions of dollars into the New Education System, or NES, to supercharge standardized test scores with extra support staff, higher teacher salaries, longer school days and new equipment. HISD budget documents reveal the estimated additional cost to adopt the reforms is about $700,000 per NES school in the first year and about $2,200 more per student at those campuses in the years after.

At the same time, Houston ISD has lost tens of thousands of students since the takeover began in 2023 as enrollment declines at a rate faster than any of its urban peer districts, translating into roughly $190 million in less state funding in that time, according to a Texas Tribune analysis.

Texas didn’t give Houston public schools extra dollars for the state intervention. Since the start of the takeover, HISD leaders quickly drained much of its massive rainy day reserves and put up dozens of district-owned buildings and land for sale. School finance experts have sounded alarms because such cost saving measures can be easily exhausted.

“That’s just a gamble,” Jonathan Travers, the CEO of Education Resource Strategies, said of districts dipping heavily into reserves for ongoing costs. “You’re just gambling that you’re going to somehow be able to raise revenue — ongoing revenue from taxpayers, from the state — in a few years to cover the gap that you’re using up your reserves to cover.”

Related: State takeovers of ‘failing’ schools are increasing, with little evidence they help students

HISD officials also shed hundreds of central office jobs and slashed transportation and social work services to curtail the shortfall in the district’s $2 billion budget. Those spending decisions were made amid parent protest, which later came to a head when voters rejected a $4.4 billion bond for building and technology updates HISD had advertised for the district’s most urgent needs.

As the state readies to end the takeover and relinquish control back to the local school board, HISD must confront how to keep its academic gains from unraveling in the face of another major transition.

“He will have stripped us of our resources,” Heather Golden, a parent whose kids graduated from HISD schools, said. “It will be almost impossible to even maintain these results because we don’t have a financial cushion anymore, especially with all the students leaving.”

The stakes of the financial strain go beyond Houston as Texas leads the nation in takeovers over poor academic performance. Since 2023, seven districts had their elected school trustees and superintendent replaced with state appointees, a pair of whom were former HISD administrators under Miles.

About a dozen more districts are at risk of the same fate. Some districts in a takeover are already changing their classrooms to mimic Miles’ strategy but without the war chest of savings that HISD had to absorb the costs.

Believers of Miles’ reform, like Eric Hanushek, an economist who studies education policy at Stanford University, say the impressive test gains justify the spending — and cutting.

Three years ago, HISD had 56 F campuses, and this year it had five. In 2025 and 2026, eight times more of NES campuses received As or Bs on the state’s grading system than they did in 2023 before the takeover.

“Not that libraries and librarians and reading and so forth weren’t valuable,” Hanushek said, but “you can’t just add on a new system and do everything you’re doing before.”

To Texas Education Commissioner Mike Morath, HISD is proof any district can adopt the reforms because Houston “is operating under the same finance system as anyone else.”

Miles told the Tribune he’s confident that Houston’s successes can last beyond the state takeover, and he believes other takeover districts are similarly well positioned. Comparing managing school finances to running a business, Miles said officials must be willing to make difficult cuts, like he said he did by right-sizing the central office. He also said he is reshaping teacher pay in ways he believes will be difficult to undo after he leaves.

“It is expensive, but we already know we can fund it,” Miles said. “We’ve been able to raise teacher salaries, to do this model. … You have to be willing to prioritize. We get a lot of pushback when we prioritize.”

Related: Do state takeovers work in Mississippi?

There are about 21,000 fewer students enrolled in HISD since the state seized control.

Houston faces the same stressors that cause enrollment declines as other urban public schools: lower birth rates, more competition and an exodus of immigrant students. But there are significant signs that the takeover itself worsened HISD’s enrollment crisis.

The share of students disappearing here has accelerated every year since the takeover started, at a rate unmatched by HISD’s peers. About 5,800 students left during the first year, about 7,400 the second and nearly 8,000 last year.

For Brooke Longoria, pulling her two children out of HISD last school year was painful. But she felt the NES model had taken the joy out of learning and left her with little choice. She enrolled them at a private Montessori school that emphasizes hands-on, project-based learning.

“It was the constant testing for me that pushed me over the edge,” Longoria said. “We do want to learn this, but … any test score increase that you’ve gained by destroying a school community, by banning books, by firing beloved principals, that’s too high a cost.”

The steepest enrollment declines were at the roughly 130 campuses that adopted Miles’ New Education System, which experience the most intense intervention, according to a Tribune analysis. While schools were already losing students prior to the takeover, enrollment decline has accelerated since.

Charter school enrollment in the Houston area rose at the same time, which experts say is an indicator that some exits reflect parent dissatisfaction with the traditional public schools.

Houston had the highest enrollment decline when the district is stacked up against comparable urban districts across the state.

A majority of students who left HISD for other public options chose charters, such as YES Prep Public Schools and KIPP Texas Schools, both of which have a longtime presence in Houston.

“They’re not moving across the state. … They may not have even moved homes at all. They’re going to a very nearby school that’s not part of HISD,” said Toni Templeton, a researcher at the University of Houston, who has analyzed the district’s enrollment. “That would lead us to believe … you’ve just made a decision to change the school.”

Angie Kemp withdrew her daughter from Browning Elementary one year after the school adopted NES. Now, she’s in the Klein school district in the northwest suburbs of Houston.

Dominika, then 6, would shut down in the middle of timed lessons, refusing to finish her schoolwork, her mom said. She would talk in her sleep about the quizzes that were 45 minutes into class so teachers could monitor students’ understanding of lessons.

“She’s a rule follower. She loves getting good grades, so it was not good seeing her like this. We knew something was wrong,” Kemp said. “We didn’t want to leave initially, but we saw the effect it was having on her.”

Related: Texas discipline push sends kids to ‘jail-like’ campuses

Texas funds public schools primarily based on student attendance. So every student that leaves translates to a loss in state dollars, shrinking the resources HISD has to provide for the children who stay.

“What we’re seeing in Houston with enrollment loss is staggering and will have a really big impact on what we can do for any of our students,” said Eileen Hairel, a parent on the community advisory council that advises the board and the superintendent. “Because, unfortunately, enrollment is money.”

The Tribune analyzed the money Houston ISD is losing based on the state’s school funding formula. The district had to adjust for a total of $190 million in losses in the first three years of the takeover.

In an interview, Miles acknowledged the financial stakes of the district’s enrollment slide. He also agreed the takeover had a part in it, though he characterized it as a “very little” factor in the drop.

“Budgets are tough and going to remain tough when you have declining enrollment,” Miles told the Tribune. “We will have declining enrollment. The question is how big. That’s a lot of money.”

As students leave, Miles and state officials said they accordingly shrink their costs by closing campuses, consolidating classes and reducing staff to match the needs of fewer students.

“When there’s declining enrollment, administrators, the board should look at ‘okay, what are we going to cut?,’” Miles said. “Whether it’s programs, whether it’s schools, whether it’s staff, … it’s in the DNA of every effective organization.”

But fewer students doesn’t automatically translate into one-for-one savings for the schools because of overhead costs they need to pay to keep the lights on and a class running, said Travers, the school finance expert from Education Resource Strategies.

“If we’ve got a first grade class with 22 kids, and we lose one student, the cost savings that we get there is maybe a little bit of food services … maybe some construction paper,” Travers said. “There’s very limited incremental change in cost until you collapse that classroom.”

As the enrollment losses force Miles to make cuts, he believes the academic gains he’s brought HISD will convince families to return.

“Parents don’t want to send their kids to a D and F school if they can help it. Now, some people are trapped, but we don’t have as many anymore, and we won’t in the future,” Miles said. “We’re bringing the pride back.”

But families such as the Holmes illustrate why it might be more complicated for the district to get enrollment to bounce back. Eric Holmes bought a house in Klein, 20 miles away from the HISD campus he withdrew his two daughters from over the focus on test-taking during the takeover.

“Because of NES, we’ve now set roots up here,” Holmes said of his family’s move. “How are you going to get them back? … I don’t see this as a sustainable model.”

As an exodus of families drains revenue, HISD is spending millions on the salaries and equipment that are the engine behind Miles’ campus overhaul.

And the superintendent had an extraordinary task: Every extra dollar he directed toward the about 130 campuses for ambitious reform would mean cuts to other parts of the district’s budget.

“I think intervention districts should get a little extra money, but we haven’t,” Miles said. “What we had to do is cut back.”

The clearest public cost estimate of Miles’ signature reforms came when Houston ISD expanded the NES model to 45 additional schools in the 2024-25 school year. District officials projected an additional $31.7 million was needed to operate those campuses during their first year, according to budget documents. That amounts to a price tag of $704,000 per campus.

Then in 2026, the district set aside about $8,500 per pupil for about 63,000 students at an NES school, compared to $6,300 for their peers at other HISD campuses. Miles said that roughly reflects a cost he expects to run “well into the future.”

In the first year of the takeover, HISD budgeted more than $96 million for technology, furniture and equipment, which primarily went to 85 NES schools. These classroom furnishings make up the physical infrastructure of Miles’ reform and are typically one-time costs.

But Miles said the largest expenses by far are adults in the classroom, including learning coaches and teacher apprentices. And those bills must be paid every year.

Teachers at NES schools also get a higher starting salary compared to the rest of the district, which accounts for working longer days. NES teachers are awarded an extra $3,000 or $9,000, depending on the subject they teach.

HISD also had to spend heavily for recruiting, hiring and training after the takeover prompted higher teacher turnover, which is nearly double the state average at 33% in the 2025-26 school year. Research from the Learning Policy Institute estimates that replacing a teacher costs about $25,000 in a large district.

As these costs add up, Miles has worked to close the gap between higher spending and lower revenue. The district still ended 2024-25, the most recently audited school year with a $311 million budget shortfall. It was the first budget shortfall the district had incurred in a decade, and every year since, the district has continued to project budget gaps.

Miles heavily dipped into the unusually large operating reserves he inherited, drawing down nearly $450 million dollars in his first years at the helm. He depleted those savings at a rate faster than HISD’s district peers.

Houston’s savings previously covered seven months of spending, but after 2024-25 were enough for three months, a notch above what the state considers a healthy buffer. Reserves provide a district a financial cushion to launch a new initiative or absorb a temporary budget shortfall during unforeseen emergencies such as the pandemic or a hurricane. They are not intended to support recurring expenses.

“Drawing down reserves is typically a very short-run strategy, unless the pool of reserves is very, very deep,” said Lori Taylor, a school finance researcher at Texas A&M University. “Once those reserves are gone, they’re gone.”

Related: Four takeaways from our investigation into Texas discipline schools

School finance experts said districts built up reserves by 2023 in anticipation of federal pandemic relief funds expiring, a position districts entering a takeover today may not be in.

Miles said his administration dipped so heavily into reserves because of the financial position his predecessors left the district in, particularly with their spending of pandemic-relief funds on “bloated” administration.

He defended using reserves for salaries and didn’t rule out leaning on it in the coming years.

“Drawing down the fund balance a little bit to pay for [recurring expenses] is not crazy behavior. It’s actually smart,” he said, adding that the district has been able to stay above the recommended reserve limit.

Meanwhile, HISD is selling property to raise money. Nearly 30 buildings or land owned by the district has been put on the market since 2025. It is not publicly available how many of these properties have sold, though Miles said revenue from that did not make a big enough difference to close the budget shortfall.

There’s a ceiling to how much school systems can lean on such sales for liquidated cash, experts said. Districts have a finite amount of real estate — and not all of them have valuable surplus to sell.

HISD has freed up recurring dollars by cutting elsewhere. Miles eliminated roughly 1,500 central-office positions as one of his first moves to save money, saying the prior administration put an excess into. In one year, he laid off more than 200 wraparound specialists who connected students in poverty with food and healthcare. In another, the district eliminated 85 bus routes.

“They’re having kids’ bus routes pick up three miles from their house. Not everybody has a car,” Liz Silva, an HISD parent who switched her kids from an NES school to a non-NES school, through a lottery system that allows families to apply to any school they are not zoned for. “You can’t talk about what you’re doing for people who are less advantaged in life, and then also do all of these things that in no way help them.”

The lack of community backing around his spending culminated in 2024 when Miles asked voters to approve a $4.4 billion school bond to pay for upgrading school buildings and technology. Its overwhelming defeat at the polls was seen as a rejection referendum on his leadership and the reform he blazed through. It was also the largest Texas school bond in history to have failed.

Miles said he’s trying to put in place policies that are “sticky” and hard to undo after he leaves. For example, this year he changed how all teachers are paid to tap into a state-funded incentive system. That brought in just under $30 million in revenue.

Texas lawmakers could ease HISD’s financial strain by committing more state dollars for the academic transformation. That’s a move that community members such as Ann Eagleton have called for.

“Money is so tight,” said Eagleton, a member of Community Voices for Public Education, a group opposed to the takeover. “If TEA wants to do the experiment, they need to pony up the money for the experiment.”

Related: In Texas, high schools bet on a bright future for oil and gas careers under Trump

At the Capitol, Morath and state lawmakers who drive education policy in the state praise Miles in a way they rarely offer up to public school superintendents. To them, Houston’s jump in academic ratings — which hinges on how students do on STAAR tests — is proof Miles’ vision is key to student learning.

“If I were any superintendent, even if I had all A’s and B’s under the A-F accountability system, I would be calling [you] for the playbook,” former Sen. Brandon Creighton, a Conroe Republican who led a Senate education committee, told Miles during the last legislative session.

Now, Texas is exporting former Houston ISD leadership from Miles’ administration to lead in other takeovers, another indicator the state is betting big on Miles’ style of reform.

Morath tapped former HISD administrators Sandi Massey to oversee the state intervention in Beaumont and Ena Meyers to oversee Lake Worth’s. In Fort Worth, a former top Houston deputy, Daniel Soliz, is assisting in that district’s takeover as deputy superintendent and chief of schools.

Fort Worth ISD is in its first year of the takeover with costly practices of NES rebranded as ELEVATE. About 24 ELEVATE campuses pay teachers more, test students more frequently and standardize their lessons. The district allocated $25 million for the reform to make it happen — money that will have to be either drawn from reserves or cut from spending.

And already, the North Texas urban district saw an historic exodus of 800 teachers in the first three months of takeover. Now enrollment is well below projections, forcing state appointees to confront a budget squeeze.

“We are still spending more money than we get in, which is not a good place to be,” Peter Licata, the district’s superintendent told the Fort Worth Report. “It’s just bad math.”

Licata, like Miles, must stretch the money his district has without extra funding from the state.

As other takeover districts jump to copy Miles’ playbook, financial experts noted that smaller districts with fewer assets and leaner administrations may have to cut classroom and student services much sooner.

“One thing that Houston has going for it is it’s a very large district that can exploit economies of scale,” Taylor said. “Houston is able to move resources around within the district in a way that other school systems could only dream about.”

Austin ISD, which is on the brink of a state takeover, doesn’t have the financial buffer Houston had to absorb new expenditures incurred from intervention. The district had just over three months of reserves at the close of the 2024-25 school year. And the district’s financial state has worsened as they faced a $105 million deficit last year.

A look at other cases of school turnaround across the country offer cautionary tales. Early academic wins do not always lead to long-term sustainability, experts said.

For example, a Tennessee reform effort led to impressive test-score gains among middle schoolers. But those gains stalled when funding became hard to sustain and leadership left. The benefits for the students at the center of the reform also faded when they went on to high schools that did not offer the same intensive support.

Advocates were also quick to celebrate a reform effort out of Denver public schools — built around school choice and the closure of low-performing campuses — after graduation rates rose from 43% to 71%. But a decade later, after superintendent and school board turnover, those policies were rolled back in part over community pushback. The rapid expansion of schools also became difficult to maintain as enrollment declined, eventually forcing the district to close or consolidate campuses.

“This is not a one-shot and done,” Lam Pham, an education policy researcher at North Carolina State University, said of intervention. “There does need to be a lot of careful thinking about how we’re going to sustain this. Or else, [as] we’ve seen in many places, it just dissipates after the intense focus goes away.”

Miles’ time in the district could be ticking as the state weighs beginning the yearslong process of returning control to elected trustees.

It will be up to the elected trustees whether to keep Miles and his costly reforms.

“It is going to take years to dig out of the financial hole he’s creating, unless the Legislature makes some huge investments,” Golden, the HISD parent, said. “It feels a little bit like a death spiral right now.”

title: Rethinking the Traditional College Student
summary:
Rethinking the Traditional College Student
Joshua.Bay Tue, 09/29/2026 - 03:00 AM

A six-part podcast series with higher ed experts explores who today’s college students are and how institutions can better support the realities of their lives.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
The image of a college student who enrolls immediately after high school, attends full-time for four consecutive years and has few significant responsibilities outside school doesn’t reflect the experience of a large share of today’s students.

If the students higher education has historically called “nontraditional” make up an ever larger share of today’s college population, how should institutions change the way they define and support student success?

That question was at the center of a six-part Voices of Student Success podcast series that explored the experiences of adult learners, working students, student parents, transfer students and first-generation students—and the different ways higher education is, or isn’t, designed to accommodate their lives.

Here are the key takeaways from each conversation about how today’s college students are reshaping higher education.

Today’s college students don’t fit the traditional mold.

For generations, colleges were largely designed around the idea of an 18-year-old who enrolled straight out of high school and followed a relatively linear path to graduation. But today’s students increasingly look different, forcing institutions to rethink long-held assumptions about whom college is designed to serve.

Sara Weissman, senior reporter at Inside Higher Ed, discussed how higher education demographics have changed, why the traditional student model no longer reflects the reality on many campuses and what institutions must do to better serve today’s learners.

Weissman noted that roughly one in five college students is a parent or has childcare responsibilities, about a quarter are adult learners, and many are balancing college with full-time employment. At the same time, the number of traditional-age students is declining, prompting many institutions to reconsider what the typical college student looks like.

“We’re seeing drops in the numbers of traditional-age students, that classic 18-year-old, and so I think colleges are really courting adult learners in a new way,” Weissman said. “There’s really been a shift in who the typical college student is.”

Weissman also reflected on the language higher education uses to describe these students. While “nontraditional student” remains the most common term, she said she prefers “post-traditional” because it better captures the idea that the traditional model is no longer the norm.

“That term does speak to me a little bit because it at least signals that we’re in a point where maybe who we thought was traditional is not what’s traditional anymore,” Weissman said. “This is millions of our students. It’s not a small fringe group who aren’t having that typical 18-year-old, dorm, four-year university experience, and the terminology we use reflects how aware we are of that.”

Stopping out doesn’t have to mean giving up on a degree.

While many students stop out before earning a credential, they often plan to return. Yet re-enrolling can prove just as challenging as enrolling the first time around. As colleges look to reach adults with some college but no credential, they are rethinking how to support students whose educational journeys aren’t linear.

Terah Crews, chief executive officer of ReUp Education, a national organization dedicated to helping adults navigate re-entry into higher education, discussed why students stop out, what motivates them to return, the barriers colleges still place in their way and what it will take to build institutions that truly serve today’s adult learners.

Crews said referring to students as “stop-outs” rather than “dropouts” better reflects the reality that, for most, leaving college is a pause, not a permanent decision to abandon higher education. She noted that family responsibilities, health challenges, financial pressures and the complexity of balancing college with life circumstances often interrupt students’ educational journeys.

“The most important thing to understand is most of these learners don’t quit thinking they’re never going to come back,” Crews said. “But once they’re out for about a semester, inertia takes over and it really gets challenging.”

Recognizing that stopping out is often temporary should also shape how institutions engage students after they leave, Crews said, yet many colleges stop actively reaching out once students have been away for an extended period.

“This sort of nuance is really important, because for the vast majority of institutions, they do nothing once learners have been out for more than a year,” Crews said.

Student parents need colleges designed around their lives.

Student parents face a unique set of barriers that can shape their ability to persist and ultimately earn a degree, including finding affordable childcare and stable housing, navigating time poverty, battling financial insecurity, and working to create a sense of belonging.

Nicole Lynn Lewis, founder and chief executive officer of Generation Hope, discussed what colleges still misunderstand about student parents and the challenges they face both in and outside the classroom.

Lewis said 20 percent of undergraduates are student parents or caregiving students, underscoring that they are not a niche population in higher education, even if they are often overlooked in conversations about today’s college students.

“That’s part of the work that we have to do in higher education … to help anyone sitting around a kitchen table understand that the student-parent population is a significant population,” Lewis said. “The more awareness we bring to this, the more understanding that people have about the student-parent experience.”

She noted that student parents often juggle coursework with bedtime routines and stay up late to finish assignments, all while finding childcare and handling other responsibilities. Understanding those realities—and designing college supports around them—can have implications beyond helping individual students earn a degree, Lewis said.

“It helps people to think about all of the ancillary kinds of connected issues,” Lewis said. “Helping student parents get through college is a part of the solution to dismantling poverty. It’s part of the solution to advancing economic mobility.”

Transfer students shouldn’t have to navigate the system alone.

Millions of students begin their education at a community college and plan eventually to earn a bachelor’s degree, but moving from one institution to another can mean parsing confusing requirements, losing credits and figuring out systems that don’t always work well together.

Josh Wyner, executive director of the College Excellence Program at the Aspen Institute, and John Fink, senior research associate and program lead at the Community College Research Center at Teachers College, Columbia University, unpacked where transfer students encounter the biggest barriers and what institutions can do to create avenues that allow more community college students to earn a bachelor’s degree.

Fink noted that about a decade ago, roughly a third of community college students transferred to four-year institutions and fewer than one in five completed a bachelor’s degree within six years. Those numbers haven’t budged much since. He said that’s particularly concerning as conversations about college affordability and postsecondary access continue to take center stage.

“Students are on their own oftentimes to navigate this complex system instead of institutions working together to make it possible for students to navigate,” Fink said. “That continues to be a challenge 10 years later.”

Wyner pointed to partnerships between community colleges and four-year institutions as one way to take more of that burden off students, including through coordinated advising that begins before a student transfers.

“They’ve decided what advising touch points they need—not just to figure out what courses to take in community college or maybe transfer, but all the way through to the bachelor’s degree,” Wyner said. “It’s those kinds of partnerships, those kinds of models, that every higher ed institution ought to be looking at.”

First-generation students are not a monolith and shouldn’t be defined by what they lack.

Being the first in your family to attend college can mean entering an unfamiliar system without the same knowledge or networks as some of your peers—from knowing where to turn for help to managing financial aid, academics and the unwritten rules of campus life. But first-generation students also bring their own experiences, strengths and support systems with them.

Hope Pacheco, associate dean of students and executive director of the Gator Resource Center at the University of Houston–Downtown, discussed what first-generation students experience when they arrive on campus, whom they turn to when they need help and what colleges can do to make sure they don’t have to figure it all out on their own.

Pacheco said institutions often lump first-generation students together, but they aren’t a monolith.

“What I feel like we’re missing is the nuances of our traditional-age students, adult learners and older students who are coming back to complete a degree, and they can all be first-gen students as well,” Pacheco said. “[There are] nuances of what a first-generation college student experience is going to look [like] … across the age and the time that they’re coming to us.”

At the same time, Pacheco said, colleges shouldn’t define first-generation students only by the knowledge or experiences they may lack. Many are already advocates for their families and arrive on campus with skills they’ve developed in other parts of their lives.

“The advocacy skills that [first-gen] students bring is important,” she said. “Even as we talk about students maybe not having the college knowledge, they’re coming to us with financial skills, they’re coming to us with skills that they’re having to not only blaze a trail to be the first, but also be a role model to their own family.”

Colleges need to design for the students they actually serve.

Adult learners, working students, student parents, transfer students and first-generation students are often grouped under the broad umbrella of “nontraditional” students. While their experiences differ, they also highlight the various ways higher education is, or isn’t, designed around the realities of their lives.

Many of these students are navigating similar pressures: balancing college with work and family responsibilities, managing financial challenges, and figuring out systems that weren’t necessarily built for them. And as these experiences become increasingly common across higher education, they raise a bigger question: If so-called nontraditional students reflect the reality of today’s college population, does it still make sense to call them nontraditional?

Bryan Ashton, chief strategy and growth officer at Trellis and head of Trellis Strategies, a nonprofit organization that works with colleges and universities across the country, discussed what today’s students need and how colleges can better design around their lives.

Ashton noted that employment can create a push and pull for students who need to work to afford college and their broader living expenses, even when their jobs make it more difficult to fit classes into their schedules.

“We know that [students] need to work to be able to close those gaps, but oftentimes employment and class schedules can come into conflict,” Ashton said. “Something that we lose a lot in conversation is this isn’t just students that are engaging with one employer; they’re engaging with sometimes two employers or multiple gig employers.”

For Ashton, the larger takeaway is that institutions need to flip their perspective: Instead of asking students to fit their lives into an institution’s model, colleges should ask how they can make that model fit into students’ lives.

“If we can begin to ask that question as we’re looking at institutional policies or as we’re looking at the experience that students are having on campus, that can become a really good test to say, ‘Are we evolving to meet the needs of modern learners?’” Ashton said.

full_text:
Under the letter “B” in the index at the back of Carlo Rovelli’s latest book you will find Francis Bacon, bats, behaviourism, Henri Bergson, and the big bang. This intriguing little miscellany reflects the sweeping ambition of what is perhaps Rovelli’s most overtly philosophical work to date.

Rovelli, who directs a quantum gravity research group in Marseille, has written several books on physics for the general reader, including the global bestseller Seven Brief Lessons on Physics. His latest is an attempt to integrate principles and theories from the discipline into a broader Weltanschauung: one of the essential unity of all things, and the profoundly relational and perspectival nature of the universe. “Electrons and minds, stones and laws, judgments and galaxies do not essentially differ in nature from one another,” he writes. “They are notions that illuminate each other.”

If this sounds familiar, that’s because it is. Rovelli echoes concepts that have been around for millennia in ancient thought, including Hinduism and Buddhism, from whose sacred texts he quotes. But what sets him apart from the countless other modern writers, dreamers and thinkers who preach the oneness of it all is that he grounds his ideas in scientific theory rather than theology or new age conjecture.

On the Equality of All Things is a slender volume holding an extraordinary density of ideas. Translator Simon Carnell, himself a poet, maintains the clarity and concision we have come to expect from Rovelli’s writing. In six chapters, or “lessons”, Rovelli lays out the philosophical significance of what he believes is a major scientific revolution, happening right now. The first lesson refers to his theory of relational quantum mechanics to ask us to abandon the notion that the world is made up of things with fixed properties. Rather, physical systems have properties relative to other physical systems. Also, everything’s moving, all the time, and there’s no fixed point around which we are in motion.

The second lesson takes aim at the idea of linearity. Rovelli urges us to accept circularity and question the need to identify the ultimate foundation of things, when in fact, it’s turtles all the way down. The lessons continue. The world is not made up of things at all, but processes. “Even a stone is a process”, and so are we. Time itself is mutable and passes at different speeds in different places. Our knowledge of anything can only ever be partial.

It’s enough to give you vertigo, and Rovelli admits it. “The resulting image of reality is haunting. Every fact is only a fact relative to something else, and even the fact that a fact is relative to something else is itself relative. There is no ground floor.” Yet, in contrast to the bleakness that can shroud such unflinching scientific accounts of the universe, Rovelli’s telling validates our messy, subjective human experiences. “None of this prevents us from describing the world from one perspective. Ours.” But the physics tells us that our perspectives are just that, and that there may be others.

On the Equality of All Things takes its place as part of a blossoming movement that asks us to see the world as a set of interconnected relationships. As such, it sits alongside the work of mycologist Merlin Sheldrake, botanist Robin Wall Kimmerer, physiologist Denis Noble and nature writer Robert Macfarlane. Rovelli’s emphasis on perspective and relationality in physics echoes similar intellectual turns in social anthropology, ecology and biology that invite us to stop thinking about the world as something we stand without, and instead take our rightful place within it. Distancing himself from the more hubristic elements of the Enlightenment – an emphasis on certainty, linearity, and overconfidence in the imperfect instrument that is Reason – Rovelli asks us to embrace “the nimble lightness of circularity, complexity, ambiguity, metaphors, emotions, the acceptance of uncertainty and change”.

His refusal to denigrate human culture as being inferior to or incompatible with hard science is refreshing. He observes wryly that the term “consciousness” has superseded the word “soul” because it is perceived to be more scientific, even though it is just as nebulous. Provided we understand that physical processes underlie everything, Rovelli sees no reason why we may not “calmly speak of the soul and emotions just as we speak of tables even if tables are collections of atoms”.

For all Rovelli is a gifted communicator, some of the science in this book required a level of intellectual scaffolding that, alas, my rusty physics A-level did not provide. At his explanation of loop quantum gravity, my brain started to creak and let off steam. Yet, even if you don’t have the foggiest idea what the granularity of spacetime means, engaging with this book as an internally coherent work of philosophy and literature is rewarding enough. And Rovelli’s conclusion is powerful: we are physical systems dancing among other physical systems, and the world “is our blood brother”. We’re at home, among family. Perhaps it’s time we honoured that kinship.

title: The federal law aimed at protecting college students from sexual abuse
summary: The lawsuit by a former Cornell University student, alleging she was raped in 2024 by seven male students, has renewed long-standing concerns about how colleges deal with sexual assault.
full_text:
When colleges receive reports of sexual assault on a student, a federal law dating back to 1972 is supposed to ensure that they investigate, and take steps to protect those students.

It's called Title IX, and it's aimed at prohibiting discrimination in schools based on sex. The law says a university must allow all students to have a safe campus environment, and that sexual violence doesn't hinder a student's equal access to an education.

It's supposed to offer students protection in cases such as the one at issue in the lawsuit by a former Cornell University student, referred to as Jane Doe. The lawsuit claims that she was drugged and raped by seven students at a fraternity house in October 2024.

The campus police investigated the incident and referred the case to the local district attorney. Though no criminal charges resulted from that investigation, the student's report triggered the campus Title IX process at Cornell.

The lawsuit states that in May 2025, at least 12 hearings were held before a panel of faculty and staff.

Cornell said in a statement that its investigation took "several months." As a result, the university said there were expulsions and suspensions, and the fraternity chapter involved "was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus."

A path for complaints by students

Title IX investigations can work in parallel with a criminal investigation, explains Beth Gellman-Beer, who spent nearly two decades at the U.S. Education Department's Office for Civil Rights.

"The school's role in Title IX, as opposed to criminal proceedings, is to determine whether or not the person accused of this sexual assault should remain on campus," she says. "Schools are not determining if somebody is going to go to jail. The school's responsibility is to ensure a safe and inclusive environment where all students have access to the educational environment."

Title IX sets a lower burden of proof than a criminal case, and it can be another route for a student to seek justice if prosecutors don't end up picking up the case, Gellman-Beer adds.

Depending on the severity of the incident being investigated, Title IX outcomes can include, in addition to suspension or expulsion for the accused, steps like providing a student victim with different housing, establishing a "no-contact" order, or creating a work schedule so that student victim and perpetrator don't work at the same time.

The goal, Gellman-Beer says, is to provide support to the victims so that they can still go to class.

Changes to Title IX

In recent years there have been big changes to how Title IX is implemented. In 2020, the Trump administration raised the burden of proof – and also required schools to conduct "live hearings with cross-examinations" – among other changes.

The Biden Administration sought to expand Title IX by including protection for LGBTQ students and by removing the requirement for hearings, as critics charged that it stifled students' willingness to report incidents.

The Trump administration this week overturned those additional protections and reverted to the 2020 version of the law.

The back and forth has created confusion at colleges about Title IX and how they should implement it.

"It's often a flawed process," says Carolin Guentert, a lawyer who has represented victims in Title IX cases involving sexual assault allegations.

"Title IX coordinators or individuals tasked with investigating these kinds of situations don't have the proper training, and are not always trauma-informed," she says. "The regulations are changing so quickly and schools' policies have to keep up." She says that can lead to an investigator being "out of step with their own schools' policies"

'Everywhere, all the time'

Meanwhile, sexual assault on college campuses remains a major problem.

"I hear a lot of people talking about, 'How could this happen at such an elite institution?'" says Guentert. "And really the answer is, this happens everywhere, all the time."

At Cornell, a 2025 survey found that more than 1 in 3 undergraduate women reported experiencing a sexual assault at some point during their time there, up from 23% in 2023.

The school created a task force to make recommendations on how to curb sexual violence on campus – which included increased knowledge about sex and school-specific processes for reporting behavoir.

Historically, a student who believes their college has failed to protect them, by not upholding Title IX, could file a complaint with the Education Department's Office of Civil Rights (OCR), which would trigger an investigation.

In its efforts to eliminate the Education Department, the Trump administration has drastically cut back that office, transferring many of its lawyers to the Justice Department.

The administration has also focused its Title IX enforcement much more heavily on gender identity and transgender athletic policies.

title: NEET-UG to shift online? Centre works on nationwide CBT infrastructure strategy
full_text:
NEET-UG may shift online as Centre develops nationwide CBT infrastructure strategy

NEW DELHI: The ministry of education is developing a nationwide Computer-Based Testing (CBT) infrastructure strategy to enable the transition of NEET from its current pen-and-paper format to an online examination, officials said. While NEET has so far been conducted in pen-and-paper mode, the National Testing Agency (NTA) conducts several other examinations, including JEE-Main, Common University Entrance Test (CUET)-UG and PG, UGC-NET and CSIR UGC-NET, in computer-based mode. Once the infrastructure strategy is in place, the plan is to shift all entrance examinations to the online mode. "A national examination-grade Computer-Based Testing infrastructure strategy is being formulated to close the geographic gap in test-centre availability, standardise centre-level examination-grade specifications and to permit the migration to CBT from the pen-and-paper mode examinations. The strategy is under active consideration based on a multi-model sourcing architecture," a senior Ministry of Education official was quoted as saying by PTI. The move comes amid an ongoing overhaul of the National Testing Agency (NTA), the nodal autonomous body responsible for conducting NEET-UG and other entrance examinations for higher educational institutions. "The possible migration of NEET (UG) from the pen-and-paper mode to CBT, including the design of the transition, the sequencing, the infrastructure prerequisites, and the equity implications for rural, women and low-connectivity-district candidates, is being worked upon. However, the recommendations of the High-Level Task Force on exam reforms in structured consultation and concurrence of the Health Ministry and National Medical Commission, are awaited," the official said. Following the NEET paper leak earlier this year, the Centre announced that the medical entrance examination would be conducted in Computer-Based Test (CBT) mode from next year. Officials aware of the development said the plan is under active consideration, but a final decision will be taken only after the report of the Nandan Nilekani-led task force set up to overhaul India’s public examination system is received. The leak of the NEET-UG medical entrance examination paper earlier this year triggered nationwide student protests and led to the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. A day after Pradhan’s resignation, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the formation of a high-powered task force headed by Infosys co-founder Nandan Nilekani to recommend reforms aimed at making the examination system leakproof.

title: Democracy without choice: how unopposed Maharashtra rural polls silence dissent
summary: The culture of unopposed elections has taken root in hundreds of villages across Maharashtra.
full_text:
Amid ongoing debates over the special intensive revision (SIR) drive by the Election Commission, name deletions, and electoral transparency, a quiet disenfranchisement persists at the grassroots level in Maharashtra -- where some local panchayats have not held elections for as long as 70 years. In these villages, the local leadership ensures that all members of the gram panchayat are chosen “unopposed”, bypassing the ballot box entirely.

In Angar town of Solapur district, a gram panchayat election hasn’t been held in 60 years. Even when the village was upgraded to a nagar panchayat last year due to population growth, leadership remained uncontested.

“We don’t have local elections; our people only vote for the Assembly and Lok Sabha. We have stood united for all these years, and people have faith in our family,” said former MLA Rajan Patil, whose family has controlled local politics for generations.

Over the decades, the politically versatile family has transitioned through the Congress, the Nationalist Congress Party, and currently, the BJP.

Succeeding his late father Baburao, Mr. Rajan Patil now shares political power with his sons, Ajinkya and Vikrant, while his daughter-in-law, Prajakta, was elected unopposed as the nagar panchayat’s first president last year.

However, the transition stirred controversy after opponents alleged that aspiring candidates were threatened and pressured not to run, accusations the Patils strongly deny.

From 2022: Contextualising Ambedkar’s idea of a moral democracy

Unopposed culture

This culture of unopposed elections has taken root in hundreds of villages across Maharashtra. Mr. Rajan Patil defends the practice, arguing that competitive elections divide communities, waste money, and hinder development.

A similar dynamic unfolds in Perid village in Kolhapur district. With a population of about 3,000, Perid has not held a contested gram panchayat election since 1956, leaving the local Patil family in charge.

“This is our tradition, where all villagers come together and decide who should be the member of the gram panchayat. In the last election, one person went against this tradition and an election was held for one of the nine seats, but he didn’t even turn up to vote,” says deputy sarpanch Shivaji Patil.

He added that this unopposed election culture extends beyond village politics to local milk societies and other cooperative bodies.

Explaining the origins of this culture, Mr. Shivaji Patil said that to prevent bitterness in village communities that arise from political feuds tearing apart families and social bonds, their forefathers decided to opt for this model of unopposed polls.

This tradition has been preserved by numerous communities now celebrated as model villages for water conservation and rural development. Among them are Padma Bhushan social activist Anna Hazare’s Ralegan Siddhi and Padma Shri awardee Popatrao Pawar’s Hiware Bazar in the Ahilyanagar district.

Voices of dissent

Mr. Popatrao Pawar has long insisted that village decisions be made unopposedly in the gram sabha so that the community acts as a united front.

However, voices of dissent have emerged in recent years across many villages, including Hiware Bazar and Ralegan Siddhi. While panels backed by Mr. Hazare and Mr. Pawar won the 2021 elections, opposition panels still contested, breaking the streak of complete unanimity.

Kolhapur-based political analyst Dr. Ashok Chousalkar noted that the concept of unopposed panchayat elections is not new, nor is it necessarily a healthy sign of democracy. He pointed out that Maharashtra’s cooperative sector, particularly sugar cooperatives, adopted this culture to suppress dissenting voices.

“Of course, there are some villages where all residents are taken into confidence for unopposed elections, but these are rare cases,” he said. “In the majority of villages, the dominant political family makes the decisions and uses its full power to suppress any opposition,” Dr. Chousalkar added.

Marginalised in politics

Alka Kamble, former sarpanch of Waghapur-Lasina in the Vidarbha region’s Yavatmal district, argued that marginalised communities suffer the most under this culture of unopposed politics.

Village bigwigs generally manage unopposed elections by selecting compliant members who offer no opposition. When seats are reserved for women, particularly Dalit and other backward class women, active women are completely sidelined in favour of candidates who will not raise their voices.

“I have been demanding that if we go for unopposed elections in our village, the decision must not be imposed by bigwigs in the village. It should be unanimous” Ms. Kamble said.

title: UEL launches US institution with Florida degree offer
summary:
The London university will offer one-year bachelor’s completion routes and master’s degrees through its new US institution, with degree teaching starting in January 2027.

The post UEL launches US institution with Florida degree offer appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The University of East London has launched a private, not-for-profit institution in Florida, opening a new route for US learners to complete bachelor’s degrees and pursue postgraduate study.

UEL USA has been granted an institutional licence by the Florida Commission for Independent Education. Undergraduate and master’s teaching will begin in January 2027, following the start of professional and executive education courses in November 2026.

A partnership with Indian River State College will enable holders of the college’s two-year associate degrees to progress into one-year bachelor’s completion programmes in digital media and communication enterprise, applied behavioural science, and business management and innovation.

Initial academic operations will be based in south Florida, including facilities at Fort Lauderdale’s Chase Stadium with the Global Institute of Sport. UEL USA will also operate at campuses owned by Indian River State College, which serves more than 24,000 students on Florida’s Treasure Coast.

“Knowledge alone is no longer enough in today’s rapidly shifting global economy,” said Amanda Broderick, UEL’s vice-chancellor and president.

“Launching UEL USA marks a transformative leap in our Vision 2028 strategy, extending our unapologetically careers-first model directly into Florida.”

Alongside the undergraduate routes, UEL USA will offer six one-year master’s programs: cyber security engineering, public health, marketing, media and communication industries, esports management, and a professional MBA.

Its professional and executive education provision will cover 19 areas. UEL said it was working with employers to tailor courses to workforce needs, including staff development and leadership training.

Heather Belmont, provost of Indian River State College, said the partnership would broaden access to further study in the region.

“The bachelor’s and master’s programs address fields with clear relevance to today’s economy, and the professional and executive education programs give working people flexible opportunities to strengthen specific capabilities,” she said.

“Together, the institutions can connect our community with international ideas while building the talent local employers need.”

By bringing together education, employers and innovation partners, this initiative can create new opportunities for students and businesses on both sides of the Atlantic

Keith Scott, British Consulate General Miami

The expansion comes as the UK seeks to grow transnational education and overseas partnerships under its refreshed international education strategy, which includes an ambition to increase education exports to £40 billion a year.

Sector action plans published in September by members of the UK’s Education Sector Advisory Group identify international market development, commercial collaboration and overseas delivery as areas for action through to 2030.

Keith Scott, Britain’s consul general in Miami, welcomed the launch as an opportunity to deepen UK-Florida ties.

“By bringing together education, employers and innovation partners, this initiative can create new opportunities for students and businesses on both sides of the Atlantic.”

title: How Colleges Are Using Technology To Attract Students on Campus Visits
summary:
Prospective students and their families have been known to judge an institution based on first impressions. In fact, 86% of higher education enrollment leaders said campus visits are the defining factor in securing enrollment, with smaller schools relying on campus visits the most, according to the 2026 State of Higher Education Pulse Survey from Niche.
The campus visit is an opportunity for institutions to put their best technological foot forward. When enrollment leaders and IT professionals work together effectively to coordinate technical infrastructure with admissions goals, they can…
full_text:
“Aside from high-quality content, you’ve got to have the right mix of hardware displaying your visuals too,” Gandu says. When Wichita State recently worked to improve the campus visit experience at its Marcus Welcome Center, the team made its biggest investment in a digital 20-by-5-foot LED video wall for daily use in official campus visit presentations.

“Our presentation room is where families are building their initial impressions of the university so we wanted to have the technology in the room that would deliver the brightest colors, booming sound and sharpest pictures,” Gandu says. Additional digital screens supplement the experience by showcasing campus visitors’ names, alumni profiles, and alumni artifacts.

At Maria College in Albany, N.Y., virtual reality is an important vehicle for education, particularly in the college’s healthcare programs. That hands-on approach extends to the admissions experience through the Center of Academic Innovation, where campus visitors get to experience virtual reality demonstrations based on their interests.

“A common introduction is a guided nursing simulation in which participants enter a virtual patient care setting and work together on a task,” says Kevin Rivenburg, executive director of enrollment management. “Each experience gives prospective students a concrete sense of what they would learn in a particular program and how that learning connects to the work they could eventually do.”

At Maria College, the IT team is onsite during campus visits to set up the virtual reality equipment and troubleshoot any issues.

Because visitors are introduced to the same software current students use in laboratory assignments and clinical preparation, they leave with an understanding of how they would learn at Maria College and an ability to picture themselves in the program, Rivenburg says.

Universities Rely on IT Partners To Deliver First Impressions

To make first impressions that resonate with visitors, admissions teams must rely on their IT counterparts. Wichita State’s Gandu and his team depend on the campus Media Resources Center for “everything from hardware to installation to media players to connectivity to ordering,” he says. “The expertise of our team is to deliver the content to our guests, not to build the tech infrastructure behind the scenes.”

Gandu shared his vision for the ideal guest experience with IT leaders, and they came back with tech recommendations and pros and cons. Their input gave the admissions team “the confidence we needed to make the tech work in our space,” Gandu says.

At Maria College, Jason Coley, director of the Center for Academic Innovation, leads the hands-on VR portion of a campus visit with support from CAI technicians. Because of the types of experiences offered to visitors, IT collaboration is needed, Rivenburg says.

DISCOVER: Virtual reality experiences help students hone their soft skills.

“The IT team prepares the equipment, helps visitors with headset fitting and controls, and guides them through the activity while explaining its connection to coursework and professional practice,” Rivenburg says. “Staff also need to recognize when someone is having technical difficulty and when they need help understanding what the simulation asks them to do. For prospective students encountering VR for the first time, this specialized support makes the experience approachable and gives them an early sense of how Maria would help them learn.”

Collaboration Between Admissions and IT Departments is Crucial

IT teams can make an important difference in the campus visit experience, but it takes partnering with admissions teams to achieve shared goals. Consider these tips for working together to build memorable campus visits:

Take time to listen. Enrollment leaders probably have a specific vision for the visitor experience they want, as well as a required budget, Gandu says. IT leaders can be better partners when they understand the vision.

Share your expertise. IT teams may know about cost-efficient technologies that can deliver the desired experience, while the admissions team may not realize the specific technology exists. “Enrollment professionals are under a lot of pressure to shape classes for their institutions, but they need campus tech experts along to help command a potent, visual storytelling experience for visitors,” Gandu says.

Involve other teams. In some cases, designing the ideal campus visit experience requires help from additional stakeholders. For example, Maria College seeks input from those who teach with and support simulation technologies, as well as IT and admissions leaders, to develop the right immersive experiences for prospects.

Keep the focus on the prospective students. “The aim is for prospective students to leave able to picture themselves learning at the college, with a clearer understanding of the career they are considering and how we would help them prepare for it,” Rivenburg says.

title: Don’t just watch: interactive video is getting interesting for higher ed
summary: Interactive video is giving prospective students more control over how they explore universities, courses and campus life. From clickable course galleries and social ads to immersive campus tours and recruitment games, we look at how universities are experimenting with the format.
full_text:
Higher education is getting really good at video.

We've seen it in campus tours, student stories, course explainers, day-in-the-life TikToks, Open Day highlights.

There's certainly no shortage of things for prospective students to watch.

But what if they could actually do something with that video, like choose the course they want to explore, tap through different study options, look around a campus in 360 degrees, find out about accommodation, or even jump straight to application information?

That's where some universities and colleges are really innovating, with interactive video games.

They're building interactive advertising campaigns and virtual campus experiences, interactive prospectuses, and even recruitment games.

So, what exactly is interactive video?

The simplest distinction is that normal video asks you to watch, while interactive video asks you to participate.

That interaction can be relatively simple: a clickable call-to-action, an information panel, a poll or a gallery that opens alongside the video.

Or it can go much further.

Viewers might choose between different paths, tap hotspots, swipe to reveal information, or move around a 360-degree environment.

They give prospective students some control over the experience.

Which makes sense, really, because prospective students rarely have just one question.

A student might be interested in Computer Science, but also want to see the campus and where they'd live, or look at scholarships and find out how to apply.

One two-minute brand video, as good as it is, can't necessarily anticipate that journey.

But an interactive experience can let the student shape it for themselves.

Interactive or immersive? There is a difference

Interactive and immersive are two terms that are often bundled together, but they're not quite the same thing.

An interactive experience requires the viewer to do something. An immersive experience tries to make them feel as though they're somewhere.

A 360-degree campus tour is a good example of immersion.

Instead of watching someone else walk around campus, prospective students can look around for themselves.

Add clickable locations, student videos, or course information and the experience becomes interactive too.

VR can take this further, but you don't necessarily need a headset or a huge production budget to make video more participatory.

And increasingly, some of that interaction can happen right inside an ad.

There's some interesting research behind it

Research highlighted by City St George's, University of London looked at 250 mobile advertising campaigns involving almost 270,000 consumers.

They identified three particularly effective forms of interaction:

Browse: "Browse" lets people explore things such as hotspots and galleries.

Sample: "Sample" gives them a virtual experience of something.

Play: "Play" brings gaming or choice into the experience.

All three increased brand choice in the study, but play produced an average increase of 36.6%, while browsing only 31.5% and sampling only 29.6%.

Those figures aren't from higher education campaigns, so we shouldn't assume that adding a quiz to an admissions ad will suddenly increase applications by 36.6%.

But the behaviours themselves translate rather neatly:

Browse your courses.

Sample life on campus.

Play with different routes through a student story.

You can probably already think of content on your website that fits each one.

The University of Tasmania puts interactive advertising into practice

One higher education examples comes from the University of Tasmania.

The University worked with Pivotus and VDX.tv on an interactive video campaign designed to engage prospective students and encourage them to explore courses and the application process.

Instead of expecting one video to do everything, the ad gave students different ways to continue exploring.

A Video tab introduced the University and Tasmania, a Courses tab opened an interactive gallery where students could browse individual courses, and an Apply section provided information about online study, financial support, and applying.

The interaction wasn't bolted on to make the ad look clever; it answered the questions a student might naturally have after watching it.

University of Tasmania created a video-powered campaign with Pivotus & VDX.tv to drive prospective student engagement. Source: https://www.vdx.tv/case-studies/university-of-tasmania

According to VDX.tv, the campaign recorded a video completion rate 26% above benchmark, a click-through rate 150% above benchmark, and average time spent 37% longer than benchmark.

For higher ed marketers, there's a useful idea here: don't just think about how to get someone to watch your video, think about what you want them to do while you've still got their attention.

Interactive video doesn't have to be a complicated choose-your-own-adventure film. It can also be making useful information around the video much easier to explore.

Gonville & Caius has replaced the printed prospectus

Interactive video doesn't have to live inside paid media either.

It no longer produces a printed prospectus. Instead, prospective undergraduates are directed to an interactive video guide.

Gonville & Caius College has done away with the paper and digital prospectus

and gone interactive.

The experience brings together perspectives from students, and faculty and staff members, giving prospective applicants a way to explore the College digitally rather than working through a traditional linear publication.

There's something very appealing about this idea, it feels warmer and more personable.

A prospectus is supposed to help a prospective student explore. Why shouldn't they control the route?

Then there's immersion.

Students can put a phone into a cardboard VR viewer and look around experiences including campus events, classes, residence halls and outdoor activities. They can also view the videos without a headset.

There's a very practical recruitment problem behind all of this: how do you give someone a meaningful sense of place when they can't visit?

Rather than simply showing prospective students what Vermont looks like, the University gives them some control over where they look.

Very useful for international recruitment and any colleges or universities drawing significant numbers of students from outside their immediate region.

Bucknell University takes a slightly different approach with its Virtual Welcome Center.

The University describes it as its "Admissions lobby, right on your screen". It combines videos, photo galleries, digital admissions materials, a customisable viewbook and a 360-degree virtual campus tour.

It isn't an interactive video ad, technically, but it shows what could happen after someone interacts with one.

The ad doesn't have to contain the whole experience, it could just be used to get the right student into a much richer one.
